Man, Phantasy Star Online was AWESOME...

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-_dWalQdIN0

See when you started the game, you had a choice to play as a Human, a Newman which was sort of a mutated human, or a Cast which was a sentient robot.

Once you picked your race, you chose your class, you could choose to be a Hunter and specialize in close up melee style combat. A Ranger that stayed back and sniped and used heavy weapons or a Force which specialized in support magic, offensive spells, etc.

The name you assigned your character also determined your Section ID. Your Section ID determined which rare weapons were available to you and which ones were not. Getting the "right" Section ID was important if you wanted to find the "Good" weapons. Some people would get multiples of the most sought after guns. Other people could get anything BUT that gun.

When you'd teleport down to the play area, there were 4 to choose from that you unlocked one at a time. The Forest was green and full of plants, the Caves were underground and filled with stalactites and stalagmites, the Mines were populated with intelligent machines trying to kill you and the Ruins were kind of a Lovecraftian horror show.

Each level ended with a giant boss fight with multiple forms, each of which required different tactics to beat but were more or less bullet sponges.

To help with this were a bunch of weapon classes, and each weapon also had the possibility of doing elemental damage. Fire, Ice, Electricity, Earth, Light and Dark.

As you progressed through each level, you would find message capsules left behind that tell you the background and story.

Playing the game started you in a central hub called a ship that looked very much like a tower. In the tower there were shops to buy different gear and a guy called a Tekker who would identify unknown items. Unknown items would appear as a colored jewel that dropped from a slain enemy. The color would determine how rare the item was. Unfortunately, the Tekker wouldn't always give you something useful. Many times you'd fine a red (exotic) gem and turn it in only to be given an item called a Photon Drop which was really just a rare currency item you could use to buy other things.

In the centralized hub you could interact with other players, but you were limited to text chat and emotes such as dancing, sitting, pointing and waving.

Using the mission counter, you could play missions that were different from the base patrol where you just wandered through the level. The missions would often take you over the same ground repeatedly, but by grinding them you earned experience and the potential for better weapons.

You were assisted in your journey by a flying robot hovering over your shoulder. You could feed this robot items to level it up, change it's appearance and grant it special abilities. By doing (or taking!) enough damage, you would fill a super meter which could be used at will to launch a massive attack damaging most things on the screen.

There were special events and gear tied to different holidays, unfortunately these were usually limited just to Japan as Sega rarely saw fit to do them on American servers. :(

Teams were limited to 4 players at a time, but you could build a team live from a countertop in the tower. You could also lock your team, set it to friends or invitation only and password protect it to keep other people out. Or you could leave it open so anyone could see how many players it had, where you were, what you were doing and decide if they wanted to join or not.

Generally speaking, any language which has the ideology of "Only One Correct Way To Do It." is an opinionated language. So, you are going to have people talking about "The Ruby way of doing something", meaning you could do it this way, but the "Ruby way" is the way you are supposed to do it. But someone else is always deciding which way is the "correct" way. It's a matter of (someone else's) opinion and you are expected to conform to it.

In other words, there are many ways of skinning a cat, but there is a specific "Ruby Way" of skinning a cat. This culture gets much worse as you delve into Rails. I'm fairly certain Rails should be classified as a cult.

Python is guilty of being opinionated as well, but to a lesser extent.

C / C++ is the anti-thesis of an opinionated language in that it's philosophy is: "We expect our devs to be competent. They probably know what the fuck they are doing. So, do whatever the fuck you want."

First, we'd have to closely define "person."

Working from a close definition though, the answer would be pretty straightforward.

If "person" means, among other things, "member of the species homo sapiens," then the answer would be no. I have no idea at what point one could say that the being was no longer a "person," and I don't think there even is any specific demarcation point. But it would certainly be the case that one was no longer a member of the species homo sapiens when one was 100% android.

If "person" merely means "self-aware being," then, presuming the android in question was self-aware, I'd say that the answer would self-evidently be yes. I don't doubt that there are some who'd wish to dispute that, but frankly I don't think there's any reasonable argument to the contrary. If a "person" is a self-aware being, then a self-aware being is a "person." Full stop.

The more fascinating question, to me, would be whether, in a specific instance of such replacement that included some science-fictional transference of the individuals thoughts and memories to the new "container," would it still be the same person?
